intro: Buddhist texts reached English readers only in the 1800s. Translators at Oxford and London, monks in Sri Lanka and Burma, and teachers from Japan all played a part. In 1893, Buddhist speakers stood before a crowd in Chicago. In this unit, you will follow how Buddhist texts and teachers came to America.

You will meet Max Müller, the Rhys Davids, Edwin Arnold, Anagarika Dharmapala, Soyen Shaku and D.T. Suzuki, who once lived in La Salle, Illinois. Then you will follow Japanese American Buddhists through the wartime camps to new temples in Chicago in 1944, and see the immigrant temples, convert centers and mindfulness debates of today.

By the end, you will be able to explain how translators' word choices shape meaning, describe the 1893 Parliament and its Buddhist speakers, tell the story of Japanese American Buddhism and Chicago's temples, and discuss questions American Buddhists face today.
bigQuestion: How did Buddhist texts and communities come to America, and how have they been translated, kept and changed?

title: Buddhist Texts Come to America

chapters.title: Translators, Scholars and 1893
chapters.bigQuestion: How did translators, scholars and Asian Buddhist teachers bring Buddhist texts to English readers, and how did their choices shape what readers understood?

story.title: A Voice in White Robes
story.kicker: A young Sri Lankan speaker stands before a crowd in Chicago in September 1893.
paragraphs: In September 1893, Chicago was hosting the World's Columbian Exposition, a huge world's fair. Alongside it, in a new building on Michigan Avenue that later became the Art Institute, leaders of many religions gathered for the World's Parliament of Religions.

One speaker was Anagarika Dharmapala, a Buddhist from Sri Lanka, then called Ceylon, who was not yet thirty. He wore white robes. He spoke in English about the Buddha's teaching. He told the audience that Buddhism valued reason, kindness and self-effort.

Another Buddhist speaker came from Japan: Soyen Shaku, a Rinzai Zen abbot. His talk was translated into English by a young man who would become famous himself, D.T. Suzuki. It was read to the crowd in English.

For many Americans in the hall, this was the first time they had heard Buddhists explain their own tradition in person. Newspapers reported the speeches. Some listeners began to read Buddhist books, many of them recent English translations.
story.think: Why might it matter that Buddhists spoke for themselves at the Parliament, rather than being described by others?

lessons.title: Max Müller and the Sacred Books of the East
lessons.mainIdea: Max Müller edited the Sacred Books of the East (1879–1910), 50 volumes of Asian scriptures in English.
reading: Friedrich Max Müller (1823–1900) was a German-born scholar at Oxford University. He studied Sanskrit and the history of religions. He believed Western readers should be able to read the scriptures of Asia in English.

Müller planned and edited the *Sacred Books of the East*, a series of 50 volumes published by Oxford from 1879 to 1910. It included Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, Chinese, Zoroastrian and Islamic texts. Müller himself translated the Dhammapada for volume 10 (1881).

The series made these texts widely available for the first time. Scholars today note that it also reflected its era: Müller chose which texts counted as 'sacred books' and treated religions as mainly about texts, not *practice*.

words.d: a 50-volume Oxford series of Asian scriptures in English (1879–1910), edited by Max Müller

lessons.title: T.W. and Caroline Rhys Davids
lessons.mainIdea: T.W. and Caroline Rhys Davids translated and published Pali texts through the Pali Text Society.
reading: T.W. Rhys Davids learned Pali from Buddhist monks while serving as a British official in Sri Lanka. He founded the Pali Text Society in 1881 and translated many suttas, including Buddhist Suttas (SBE 11, 1881).

His wife, *Caroline Rhys Davids* (1857–1942), was a scholar in her own right. She translated the Therigatha as *Psalms of the Sisters* (1909) and worked on the Abhidhamma. She later led the Pali Text Society as president.
Their work relied on Sri Lankan and Burmese monks, who taught them the language and supplied manuscripts. Historians today stress this *collaboration*, which older accounts often left out.

words.d: British scholar (1857–1942) who translated the Therigatha and led the Pali Text Society

lessons.title: The Light of Asia
lessons.mainIdea: Edwin Arnold's poem The Light of Asia (1879) told the Buddha's life in English verse and became a bestseller.
reading: In 1879, the English poet Edwin Arnold published *The Light of Asia*, a long poem about the life of the Buddha. It retold the story from the prince's birth to his awakening and teaching.

The poem was hugely popular in Britain and America, selling hundreds of thousands of copies. For many readers, it was their first picture of the Buddha. Its language made the Buddha sound like a noble Victorian hero.

Arnold's poem also mattered in Asia. Anagarika Dharmapala later said reading it moved him deeply. Scholars note that a *poem* like this shapes an image of the Buddha that is partly the poet's own; it is a *retelling*, not a translation.

words.d: Edwin Arnold's 1879 poem about the life of the Buddha
telling a story again in new words, often with changes

look.title: Translation or Retelling?
look.text: A translator tries to carry a text's words into another language. A poet retelling a story adds images, feelings and ideas of their own. The Light of Asia draws on Buddhist biographies but is Arnold's own poem.
look.prompt: Why is it important to know whether you are reading a translation or a retelling?

lessons.title: The World's Parliament of Religions
lessons.mainIdea: The 1893 Parliament in Chicago was the first large meeting where Asian religious leaders spoke to Americans in person.
reading: The *World's Parliament of Religions* met in Chicago from September 11 to 27, 1893, as part of the World's Columbian Exposition. It is often seen as the start of formal interfaith dialogue in the modern West.
Speakers included Christians and Jews as well as Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and others. The Hindu teacher Swami Vivekananda became famous for his opening words, 'Sisters and brothers of America'.

Some organizers hoped the Parliament would show Christianity as the highest religion. Asian speakers used the platform to present their own traditions on their own terms. Historians see it as a turning point in American knowledge of *world religions*, and of *interfaith* meeting.

words.d: a gathering of religious leaders in Chicago, September 1893
between or among different religions

lessons.title: Anagarika Dharmapala
lessons.mainIdea: Dharmapala, a Sri Lankan Buddhist reformer, spoke at the Parliament and worked to restore Buddhist sites in India.
reading: *Anagarika Dharmapala* (1864–1933) was born in Colombo, Sri Lanka, then a British colony. He grew up during a Buddhist revival that resisted Christian missionary schools. 'Anagarika' means 'homeless one', a title he took as a layman devoted full-time to Buddhism.

In 1891 he founded the Maha Bodhi Society to restore Bodh Gaya, where Buddhists believe the Buddha reached awakening. At the 1893 Parliament, he presented Buddhism as rational and compatible with science.

Dharmapala returned to America several times and helped spread Buddhism abroad. Some historians call his approach *Buddhist modernism*: presenting Buddhism in terms of reason and ethics for modern audiences. Sri Lankans honor him as a national hero.

words.d: Sri Lankan Buddhist reformer (1864–1933) who spoke at the 1893 Parliament
presenting Buddhism in terms of reason, science and ethics for modern readers

look.title: Speaking to a New Audience

lessons.title: Soyen Shaku and D.T. Suzuki
lessons.mainIdea: Soyen Shaku spoke for Japanese Zen in 1893, and his student D.T. Suzuki later made Zen famous in the West.
reading: *Soyen Shaku* (1860–1919) was abbot of Engakuji, a Rinzai Zen temple in Kamakura, Japan. He spoke at the 1893 Parliament, with his speech translated into English by his lay student, D.T. Suzuki.

*D.T. Suzuki* (1870–1966) then came to America. From 1897 he lived for about eleven years in La Salle, Illinois, working for Paul Carus of the Open Court Publishing Company, translating Asian texts. Carus himself had written The Gospel of Buddha (1894).

Suzuki later wrote many English books on Zen. From the 1950s, his lectures at Columbia University influenced writers, artists and thinkers. Scholars today note that Suzuki presented Zen in his own way, sometimes stressing experience over ritual and monastic life.

lessons.title: Suffering or Unsatisfactoriness?
lessons.mainIdea: Translators render dukkha as 'suffering', 'pain', 'stress' or 'unsatisfactoriness', and each choice shapes the reader.
reading: The Pali word *dukkha* is at the center of the Four Noble Truths. Rhys Davids and most early translators put it as 'suffering' or 'pain'. That made Buddhism sound gloomy to some Western readers.

Later translators argued that dukkha covers more than pain: it includes the sense that things never fully satisfy because they change. Some chose 'unsatisfactoriness'; others use 'stress' or leave the word untranslated.

Each choice brings out one side of the idea. A reader who sees only 'suffering' might think Buddhism is pessimistic. A reader who sees 'unsatisfactoriness' might think it is about mild dissatisfaction. Scholars say careful readers learn the original word and its *connotation*, or feeling.

words.d: a Pali word translated as suffering, stress or unsatisfactoriness (Sanskrit: duhkha)
the feelings and ideas a word suggests beyond its basic meaning

look.title: Three Translations of One Line
look.text: Translation A: 'Birth is suffering, old age is suffering.' Translation B: 'Birth is stressful, aging is stressful.' Translation C: 'Birth is unsatisfactory, aging is unsatisfactory.' All three render the same Pali line of Samyutta Nikaya 56.11.
look.prompt: How does each translation make you feel? Which do you think is closest to the idea taught in this unit?

check.why: Early translators used 'suffering' or 'pain'.

check.q: Why did some later translators choose 'unsatisfactoriness'?
choices: Dukkha includes the sense that changing things never fully satisfy
check.why: They wanted to show dukkha's wider meaning.

check.q: What is connotation?

check.why: Word choice changes the reader's feeling.

lessons.title: Old English, New English
lessons.mainIdea: Victorian translations used formal, Bible-like English, which shaped how early readers imagined the Buddha.
reading: Many early translators used a formal English that echoed the King James Bible, with words like 'thee', 'verily' and 'brethren'. Readers heard the Buddha speaking like a biblical prophet.

Some key words were translated with Christian terms. 'Sin', 'heaven' and 'priest' sometimes appeared where the Pali meant something different. Scholars call this *domestication*: making a foreign text sound familiar.

Modern translators often use plainer English and keep Pali terms like dukkha, nibbana and kamma with explanations. Each approach has costs and gains, and comparing translations helps a reader spot a translator's *choices*.

words.d: making a foreign text sound familiar to readers, sometimes changing its meaning
decisions a translator makes about words and style

check.q: What do many modern translators do with key Pali terms?

lessons.title: Who Speaks for Buddhism?
lessons.mainIdea: Western scholars and Asian Buddhists shaped the modern picture of Buddhism together, and sometimes disagreed.
reading: Some Western scholars in the 1800s thought the 'real' Buddhism was found in ancient texts, not in the temples, rituals and relics they saw in Asia. They sometimes judged living Buddhists as having strayed from the texts.
Asian Buddhists pushed back and shaped the picture too. Monks in Sri Lanka and Burma taught the scholars. Leaders like Dharmapala and Soyen Shaku chose how to present their traditions abroad.

Scholars today describe Buddhism as both texts and living *practice*, from chanting and offerings to festivals and meditation. They ask whose *representation* of a tradition is being given, and they include the voices of practitioners.

words.d: how a person or group is described or shown to others
what religious people actually do, such as rituals and festivals

chapters.title: Japanese American Buddhists and Buddhism Today
chapters.bigQuestion: How have Buddhist communities in America kept, changed and shared their traditions?

story.title: From a Barracks to a Temple
story.kicker: A priest leads services in a camp barracks, and years later his community has a temple in Chicago.
paragraphs: In 1942, after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, the U.S. government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast into inland camps. Most were U.S. citizens. Many were members of Jodo Shinshu Buddhist temples.

In the camps, people lived in rows of tar-paper barracks. Buddhist priests held services in whatever rooms they could find. Families chanted, listened to Dharma talks and kept Obon and the Buddha's birthday, even behind barbed wire.

Some Buddhists were watched with special suspicion, and some priests were held apart from their families. Still, the communities held together. Young people ran Sunday schools. Older members led chanting when no priest was near.

When families were allowed to leave, many moved to Chicago for work. In 1944, two new Buddhist temples began in the city: the Buddhist Temple of Chicago and the Midwest Buddhist Temple. Both still serve their communities today.
story.think: What helped these Buddhist communities hold together in the camps?

lessons.title: Buddhist Churches of America
lessons.mainIdea: Japanese immigrants brought Jodo Shinshu to America, and their organization took the name Buddhist Churches of America in 1944.
reading: Japanese immigrants began arriving in Hawaii and on the West Coast in the late 1800s. Many were Jodo Shinshu Buddhists. In 1899, two priests came to San Francisco and started what became the Buddhist Mission of North America.

Temples grew in California, Washington and Oregon. To fit American life, many used pews, hymnals, Sunday services and Sunday schools. Some called themselves 'Buddhist churches'. Services were often in English.

In 1944, while many members were still in the camps, the organization changed its name to the *Buddhist Churches of America* (BCA). Today it is one of the oldest Buddhist organizations in the United States. Scholars call such changes *adaptation*.

words.d: the national organization of Jodo Shinshu temples in the U.S., named in 1944
Shin Buddhism, a Japanese Pure Land tradition centered on Amida Buddha

lessons.title: Faith in the Camps
lessons.mainIdea: During the 1942–45 incarceration, Japanese American Buddhists kept their practice going under hard conditions.
reading: The camps were built in remote places like Manzanar in California, Heart Mountain in Wyoming and Topaz in Utah. Families lived in crowded barracks, with little privacy. There were ten main camps in all.

Buddhists faced extra suspicion because their religion was linked to Japan. Some priests were arrested early and held in separate camps. Still, Buddhist services, festivals and Sunday schools went on in the camps, often led by laypeople.

In 1988, the U.S. government formally apologized for the incarceration and paid *reparations* to survivors. Buddhist temples today keep the *memory* of the camps through services, exhibits and pilgrimages to the old camp sites.

words.d: payments made to make up for a wrong
what a community remembers and keeps alive about its past

lessons.title: Two Chicago Temples, 1944
lessons.mainIdea: In 1944, Japanese Americans leaving the camps founded the Buddhist Temple of Chicago and the Midwest Buddhist Temple.
reading: People leaving the camps could not return to the West Coast at first. Thousands moved to Chicago, where jobs were available. They started new lives in neighborhoods on the North and South Sides.

In 1944, Rev. Gyomay Kubose and others started what is now the *Buddhist Temple of Chicago*. The same year, another group founded the *Midwest Buddhist Temple*, which later built a temple in the Old Town neighborhood. Both are Jodo Shinshu temples.
The Midwest Buddhist Temple is known for its summer Ginza Holiday festival, with Japanese food, crafts and performances. Both temples offer services in English and welcome visitors.

lessons.title: Immigrant Temples After 1965
lessons.mainIdea: After the 1965 immigration law and the wars in Southeast Asia, many new Buddhist communities formed across America.
reading: The *Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965* ended quotas that had kept out most Asian immigrants. Families from Thailand, Sri Lanka, Korea, Taiwan, China and elsewhere began arriving in larger numbers.

After 1975, refugees from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos resettled across the U.S., including in Illinois. They built temples in homes, storefronts and later large buildings. These temples help keep language, food and family customs alive.

Today many immigrant temples serve as community centers too. They hold language classes, festivals and youth groups. Scholars note that these communities make up a large share of American Buddhists, even though they appear less often in the media. They are part of the *diaspora*.

words.d: a U.S. law that ended national quotas and opened immigration from Asia
a community living far from its original homeland

lessons.title: Convert Communities and Meditation Centers
lessons.mainIdea: Since the 1950s, many Americans have joined Buddhism as converts, often through meditation centers.
reading: In the 1950s and 1960s, writers and students became interested in Zen, partly through D.T. Suzuki's books. Japanese teachers such as Shunryu Suzuki founded the San Francisco Zen Center in 1962. Tibetan teachers came after fleeing Tibet in 1959.

In the 1970s, Americans who had studied in Asia founded *meditation centers* in the Theravada vipassana, or insight, tradition. Many convert Buddhists focus on meditation, retreats and study more than on rituals or festivals.

Scholars sometimes talk of 'two Buddhisms' in America: immigrant temples and convert centers. Others say this split is too simple, since many communities mix both and the children of immigrants and converts share practices.

words.d: places where people gather to learn and practice meditation
insight meditation, a practice in the Theravada tradition

look.prompt: What is similar and what is different? Why might the 'two Buddhisms' idea be too simple?

lessons.title: Public Teachers
lessons.mainIdea: The Dalai Lama and Thich Nhat Hanh became world-famous Buddhist teachers through books, talks and peace work.
reading: The *Dalai Lama*, Tenzin Gyatso (born 1935), is the 14th Dalai Lama, a leading figure of Tibetan Buddhism. He fled Tibet in 1959 and has lived in exile in India. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989.

*Thich Nhat Hanh* (1926–2022) was a Vietnamese Zen monk. He worked for peace during the Vietnam War and was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize by Martin Luther King Jr. in 1967. Exiled from Vietnam, he founded Plum Village in France.

Both wrote many books in English and spoke to large audiences. Their teachings on compassion, mindfulness and peace reached many people who are not Buddhist. Scholars note that their public images are one part of much larger traditions. The Dalai Lama leads in *exile*.

words.d: a leading teacher of Tibetan Buddhism; the 14th is Tenzin Gyatso (born 1935)
Vietnamese Zen monk and peace activist (1926–2022)
being forced to live away from one's home country

lessons.title: From Sati to Mindfulness
lessons.mainIdea: The English word 'mindfulness' translates the Pali sati, a practice described in the suttas.
reading: The Pali word *sati* means remembering or keeping in mind. T.W. Rhys Davids chose the English word 'mindfulness' for it in 1881, and the translation stuck. It appears in Buddhist verse and prose alike.

In the Pali Canon, sati is one step of the Eightfold Path, 'right mindfulness'. The Satipatthana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 10) describes four foundations of mindfulness: body, feelings, mind and mental objects.

In the suttas, mindfulness is part of a whole path that includes ethics, wisdom and the goal of nibbana. Scholars point out that modern uses of the word often focus on attention and calm and leave out that wider *context*.

words.d: the Pali word translated as mindfulness; remembering or keeping in mind
the setting that gives a word or idea its full meaning

look.title: Four Foundations
look.text: The Buddha, as the sutta presents him, tells the monks there is one direct way for the purification of beings: the four foundations of mindfulness, contemplating body, feelings, mind and mental objects.
look.cite: Satipatthana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 10); see Bhikkhu Nanamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses (1995)
look.prompt: What four things does the sutta name? What larger goal does it connect them to?

check.why: Sati is translated as mindfulness.

check.why: Rhys Davids chose the word in 1881.

check.q: Which sutta describes the four foundations of mindfulness?
check.why: The Satipatthana Sutta is MN 10.

lessons.title: Mindfulness Programs
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1979, secular mindfulness programs have spread in hospitals, schools and businesses.
reading: In 1979, Jon Kabat-Zinn started Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) at the University of Massachusetts Medical School. He drew on Buddhist meditation but taught it without religious language.

Programs like MBSR spread to hospitals, schools, sports teams and workplaces. Researchers have studied their effects on stress and attention. These programs describe themselves as *secular*, meaning not religious.

Some Buddhist teachers welcome this spread, saying it helps many people. Others worry that removing ethics and the larger Buddhist path changes the practice. Critics sometimes use the term 'McMindfulness' for programs sold only to boost productivity.

words.d: not religious; not connected to a religion
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, a program started by Jon Kabat-Zinn in 1979

look.title: Three Views
look.text: A hospital doctor says: patients in the program report less stress. A Theravada monk says: mindfulness without ethics is incomplete. A Zen teacher says: if it helps people suffer less, that is good, and some may go deeper later.
look.prompt: What is each speaker's main concern? How could you describe all three fairly?

lessons.title: Buddhism in America Today
lessons.mainIdea: American Buddhism today includes many traditions, communities and debates, from Chicago temples to meditation apps.
reading: Walk through Chicago today and you can find Shin temples from 1944, Thai and Sri Lankan temples, Vietnamese and Cambodian temples, Tibetan centers, Korean Seon temples and Zen groups. Each keeps its own *heritage*.

American Buddhists debate many questions: how to pass traditions to children, the role of women as teachers and nuns, how to include people of all backgrounds, and how to respond to the popularity of mindfulness.
From the 1893 Parliament to the temples of 1944 and the communities of today, Chicago has been part of this story. Scholars describe it as a history of both *continuity* and change.

words.d: traditions and customs handed down from the past
staying the same or connected over time
